title: Minimal SDK Embarkation Manual (sketch)
content:
Goal:
Provide the absolute minimal, copy-pasteable SDK onboarding that gets a new app from zero to a reproducible sample call + telemetry in under 10 minutes. This is a compact, opinionated sketch for a one-page quickstart and an adjunct local 'mini-runner' for iterative development.

Why this exists (context):
- We ship a lot of surface area in SDKs; customers get overwhelmed by options.
- We need a single, pragmatic path for engineers to quickly verify integration and observe cost/latency telemetry before adding advanced features.
- This document intentionally trades completeness for speed + developer confidence.

Core assumptions:
- User has node (>=18) or python (>=3.10) locally, git, and network access to hosted Redwood API.
- A single minimal credential (REDWOOD_API_KEY) exists for sandbox/testing.
- We provide a tiny local runner binary (mini-runner) that mimics the production routing and can be used offline with small fixtures.

One-minute checklist (smoke path):
1) Set env: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_test_XXX
2) Clone example app: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/example-minisketch
3) npm install && node quickstart.js  (or: pip install -r requirements.txt && python quickstart.py)
4) Confirm output: single generated text chunk + printed telemetry (latency_ms, token_count, model_name)
5) If local-only: start mini-runner: ./mini-runner --fixture small.json && rerun client pointing at http://localhost:8080

Minimal Node sample (to appear in quickstart one-pager):
const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk');
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
(async () => {
  const resp = await client.text.generate({ model: 'redwood-alpha-1', prompt: 'Summarize the user story in one sentence.' });
  console.log(resp.output[0].text);
})();

Minimal Python sample (short snippet for docs):
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.text.generate(model='redwood-alpha-1', prompt='TL;DR: what happened?')
print(resp.output[0]['text'])

Telemetry expectations (printed in quickstart):
- latency_ms: 50-800 (depends on model)
- tokens_input, tokens_output (integer)
- model: friendly-name
These three are the minimal fields we require in the quickstart output so users can reason about cost & perf immediately.

Mini-runner (developer tool):
- Purpose: deterministic dev loop with tiny fixtures, fast cold-start, optional offline mode.
- Commands: ./mini-runner --port 8080 --fixture small.json --simulate-latency 80
- Behavior: accepts same HTTP surface as hosted API, returns small baked responses, prints server-side telemetry to STDOUT for inspection.
- Use case: iterate on prompt templates, schema validation, and retry behavior without consuming hosted credits.

Suggested quickstart page layout (one-pager):
- Header: 1-line pitch + badge (sandbox)
- Prereqs: env var, node/python, optional mini-runner
- Install + run (copy-paste commands)
- Output example with expected telemetry annotations
- Troubleshooting tips (common failures + fast fixes)
- Next steps: add streaming, function calling, and structured output links

Failure-mode decision matrix (developer-facing):
- 401: missing/invalid API key -> instruct how to check env and token scope
- 4xx (bad request): show sample payload and link to quick payload validator
- 429: rate limit -> suggest client-side exponential backoff + local mini-runner to continue iteration
- 5xx/timeout: recommend automatic retry once with jitter, then fallback to cached summary (if present)

Instrumentation contract (for SDKs):
- Client MUST emit a short telemetry object for each request in dev mode: {latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, model_key, status_code} (we only require these fields in quickstart)
- SDKs should include a dev-mode flag that prints telemetry to STDOUT in compact single-line JSON for easier CI parsing.
- Mini-runner should log a server-side trace id in the response header X-RDW-TRACE for correlating client/server logs.

Developer UX microflows (short):
1) New dev: set API key -> run quickstart -> see sample output + telemetry -> happy path.
2) Integrator: wire SDK into service -> enable dev-mode -> run integration smoke -> if 429 use mini-runner for local load testing.
3) Platform engineer: run mini-runner in CI to validate prompts + detect token regressions before PR merge.

Open questions / decisions to resolve before copy-final:
- Should dev-mode telemetry be opt-in via env var or enabled by default in SDKs? (lean: opt-in but very prominent in quickstart)
- Mini-runner distribution: tiny binary vs node/python package? (lean: binary for parity with router behavior, but package for ease of hacking)
- Which model name to use in the absolute minimal example? (redwood-alpha-1 vs a 'small' curated dev model)

Proposed next actions (short roadmap):
- This week: finalize one-pager copy + 1-line telemetry example (owner: Avery)
- Next 2 weeks: land mini-runner prototype in repo, add fixture set (owner: Ravi)
- Month: user test quickstart with two external teams, collect friction points (owner: Sofia)

Notes to self / rough editorial bits (informal):
- Keep words short; new users read top-to-bottom. Avoid long API reference inside the quickstart.
- Provide playground link that auto-fills the sample prompt (reduce friction).
- Keep both Node and Python examples but favour Node for first-run copy (most sample apps use JS).
- Consider a tiny 'replay' helper that converts a logged telemetry line to a reproducible mini-runner scenario.

Pasteable troubleshooting snippets (very small):
- Check API key in bash: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY | sed -n '1p'
- Debug network: curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/ping

End of sketch — this file is intentionally compact. The one-pager should surface these few things only: install, single-run, telemetry, mini-runner. Everything else lives in deeper docs and a follow-up developer toolkit repo.
